etymology: German Wolfgang — from wolf (“wolf”) and gang (“path, going”). His surname is a Latinized form of the German Köpfel (“little head”), rendered as Capito after the Roman fashion by which Renaissance scholars dressed their names in Latin.
biblical_def: Wolfgang Capito (1478–1541 AD) was a Hebraist, humanist, and Reformer of Strasbourg, and, with Martin Bucer, one of the two chief architects of the Reformation in that free imperial city. Trained in medicine, law, and theology, and reckoned among the ablest Hebrew scholars of his age, Capito served for a time in the household of Albert of Mainz, the very prelate whose indulgence-traffic Luther had assailed; yet the light of the recovered gospel drew him out of the shadow of Rome. By 1523 he had settled in Strasbourg, cast in his lot openly with the evangelical cause, and taken a lawful wife, testifying with his life against the unscriptural yoke of enforced clerical celibacy. There he laboured alongside Bucer to plant Reformed preaching, to order the churches, and to catechize the people in the pure doctrine of justification by faith alone. Capito was, by temperament, an irenic and conciliatory man, sometimes drawn too near to the Anabaptists and to compromise in his longing for concord; but the mature course of his ministry ran in the Reformed channel of Strasbourg, honoring the sole authority of Scripture and the free grace of God in Christ. He died of the plague in 1541, a faithful under-shepherd whose Hebrew learning and patient labour helped make Strasbourg a nursery of the Reformed faith and a refuge to the persecuted.
webster_summary: Hebraist and Reformer of Strasbourg (1478–1541 AD); with Bucer the chief planter of the Reformed church in that city.
webster_full: WOLFGANG CAPITO, proper noun. German Wolfgang + Latinized Capito (from Köpfel, “little head”).

Colleague of Martin Bucer at Strasbourg; together they ordered the Reformed church of that free imperial city.
Formerly in the service of Albert of Mainz; drawn to the evangelical cause and married by 1523, forsaking enforced celibacy.
An irenic man, sometimes over-conciliatory toward Anabaptists; died of the plague in 1541.

corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of patient, learned labour joined to the pure gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: Capito is remembered, when he is remembered at all, chiefly as a lesser satellite of Bucer, and the temptation is to let his Hebrew learning and his quiet, irenic labour be swallowed up in the fame of his more forceful colleagues. That is a species of forgetfulness, not of falsification; the man himself taught no error worth naming as corruption, and his mature ministry ran soundly in the Reformed channel of Strasbourg.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What Capito recovers for us is the marriage of deep learning to a humble, peace-loving spirit poured out in the ordinary work of ordering a church and catechizing a people. His over-fondness for concord is a warning that peace must never be purchased at the price of doctrine; yet his patient scholarship and his willingness to labour in another man’s shadow rebuke our appetite for prominence and teach us to seek the good of Christ’s church rather than our own name.
roots_summary: German Wolfgang + Latinized Capito; the Hebraist Reformer of Strasbourg, colleague of Bucer.

His learning served the gospel; his Hebrew opened the Scriptures to a people newly given the word in their own tongue.
A peacemaker whose love of concord was both his grace and his snare — a warning that peace must never be bought with truth.

etymology: French Guillaume — the French form of William, from the Germanic Wilhelm (wil, “will,” and helm, “helmet, protection”). The surname Farel is of Provencal origin, borne by his family in the Dauphiné region of southeastern France.
biblical_def: Guillaume Farel (1489–1565 AD) was the fiery French evangelist and Reformer of the French-speaking Swiss lands, the man whose thundering zeal fixed the Reformation in Geneva and whose fearful adjuration compelled John Calvin to remain there. Converted under the humanist Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples, Farel forsook the errors of Rome and gave himself to itinerant, open-air preaching across Neuchatel, Lausanne, and the Vaud, overturning altars, disputing with priests, and enduring stonings, mob violence, and repeated peril of death for the gospel’s sake. He was no systematizer but a trumpet — loud, bold, tender toward Christ and terrible toward idolatry. When Calvin, then a quiet young scholar, sought only to pass a night in Geneva in 1536 on his way to a life of study, Farel sought him out and, learning of his intent, charged him in the name of Almighty God that God would curse his repose and his studies if he withheld his help from the church in her hour of need. Calvin, by his own testimony, was so stricken and terrified by this that he stayed — and the history of Reformed Geneva turned upon that word. Farel laboured on at Neuchatel to a great age, marrying late, preaching to the end, a Boanerges whose holy violence God used to plant churches that Calvin would water.
webster_summary: Fiery French Reformer of French-speaking Switzerland (1489–1565 AD); the evangelist of Geneva who adjured Calvin to stay.
webster_full: GUILLAUME FAREL, proper noun. French Guillaume (“William”) + Farel, a Provencal surname.
French evangelist and Reformer (1489–1565 AD); converted under Lefèvre d’Étaples.
Bold itinerant preacher across Neuchatel, Lausanne, and the Vaud; endured stonings and mob violence for the gospel.
In 1536 adjured John Calvin, in the name of God, to remain in Geneva — and Calvin, terrified, stayed.
A trumpet rather than a systematizer; laboured on at Neuchatel to a great age.

Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay.

But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.

corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of holy boldness in the preaching of the gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: Farel is sometimes reduced to a footnote in the biography of Calvin — the loud man who happened to be in the room when the great theologian was recruited. This is a diminishment born of forgetfulness rather than of any error in the man; Farel taught the sound Reformed doctrine of the grace of God in Christ, and his fault, if fault it was, lay only in a vehemence that could tip toward rashness, not in any corruption of the faith.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle Farel recovers for a timid age is holy boldness — the readiness to preach in the open air, to overturn idols, and to bear stones and blows for the name of Christ without counting one’s life dear. His famous adjuration of Calvin teaches us that God’s call may come through a fellow labourer’s terrible earnestness, and that a man’s plans for quiet study must bow to the church’s need. Where we prize our comfort, Farel rebukes us; where we mute the gospel for peace, his trumpet still sounds.
roots_summary: French Guillaume (“William”) + Farel; the fiery evangelist of Geneva who compelled Calvin to stay.

usage: Guillaume Farel — the trumpet of Geneva whose holy violence God used to keep Calvin at his post.
“God will curse your studies” — the adjuration by which Farel turned the course of the Reformed Reformation.
A preacher, not a systematizer; Farel planted where Calvin would water, and the church grew by both.

etymology: Latin Johannes — from Hebrew Yochanan (“the LORD is gracious”), the same name as John. The surname Brenz derives from his native region in the Swabian lands of southern Germany.
biblical_def: Johannes Brenz (1499–1570 AD) was the Lutheran Reformer of the duchy of Württemberg and of the free imperial city of Schwäbisch Hall, one of the ablest and most industrious of Luther’s Swabian disciples. A student at Heidelberg, he heard Luther defend the theology of the cross at the Heidelberg Disputation of 1518 and was won to the evangelical cause. As preacher at Schwäbisch Hall and later as chief ecclesiastical organizer of Württemberg under Duke Christoph, Brenz laboured tirelessly to reform worship, to establish sound preaching, to write catechisms for the instruction of the young, and to order church discipline — his Catechism becoming one of the most widely used in the German lands. He stood firm when persecution came, fleeing for his life more than once after the emperor’s victory over the Protestant princes, hiding as an exile while he trusted the providence of God. We honor his diligent labour for the gospel, his catechetical care for the flock, and his steadfastness under trial. Yet as a Lutheran he held, over against the Reformed, that Christ’s body is present in, with, and under the bread of the Supper by a real and bodily presence — a point on which we must, gently but plainly, own our Reformed difference, confessing with the Reformed churches that the believer feeds on the whole Christ by faith through the Spirit, and not by any carnal presence of His flesh in the elements.
webster_summary: Lutheran Reformer of Württemberg (1499–1570 AD); catechist, church-organizer, and disciple of Luther.
webster_full: JOHANNES BRENZ, proper noun. Latin Johannes (“John,” from Hebrew Yochanan) + Swabian surname Brenz.
German Lutheran Reformer (1499–1570 AD); won to the gospel at the Heidelberg Disputation of 1518.
Preacher at Schwäbisch Hall and chief church-organizer of Württemberg under Duke Christoph.
Author of a widely used catechism; a diligent labourer in reforming worship and instructing the young.
Held the Lutheran doctrine of a bodily presence of Christ in the Supper — here the Reformed differ.
scriptures: I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
Deu 6:7
And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
Joh 6:63
It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.
Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.
corruption_summary: A faithful Lutheran labourer, honored for his diligence; the Reformed part company only on the bodily presence in the Supper.
corruption_paragraphs: Brenz taught no error of the postmodern sort, and the chief thing to be marked in our voice is not a modern corruption at all but the old and honest confessional difference between the Lutheran and the Reformed touching the Lord’s Supper. Brenz was among the sharpest defenders of the Lutheran doctrine that Christ’s body, being made partaker of the omnipresence of His divine nature, is truly and bodily present in the Supper. We honor his zeal for the reality of communion with Christ while confessing, with the Reformed churches, that we feed upon the whole Christ by faith through the Holy Spirit, our souls lifted up to where He is at the right hand of the Father, and not by any bodily descent of His flesh into the bread.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from Brenz’s life is catechetical faithfulness — the patient, unglamorous work of teaching sound doctrine to the young and ordering the worship of the church. In an age that despises catechesis and mistakes novelty for life, Brenz’s labour rebukes us; and his steadfastness in exile, when he fled for his life yet kept the faith, teaches us to trust the providence of God when the powers of this world turn against His people.
roots_summary: Latin Johannes (“John”) + Swabian Brenz; the Lutheran Reformer and catechist of Württemberg.

A Reformer who fled for his life yet kept the faith — steadfast under the emperor’s hand.

etymology: German Johann — from Hebrew Yochanan (“the LORD is gracious”). The surname Gerhard is a Germanic name from ger (“spear”) and hart (“hardy, brave”), thus “brave with the spear.”
biblical_def: Johann Gerhard (1582–1637 AD) was the foremost of the Lutheran scholastic theologians, a professor at the University of Jena, and, after Luther and Chemnitz, reckoned the third in the great triad of classical Lutheran divinity. Turned toward the ministry in his youth through a grave illness and the counsel of the devout Johann Arndt, Gerhard united in a rare degree the warm, devotional piety of the heart with the rigorous, ordered learning of the schools. His monumental Loci Theologici — a vast, nine-volume body of divinity treating every head of Christian doctrine with immense patristic and biblical erudition — became the standard system of Lutheran orthodoxy for generations, mined even by later Reformed writers for its learning. He wrote also the tender Sacred Meditations, proving that the deepest scholasticism and the warmest devotion may dwell together in one man. We honor his prodigious labour, his defence of the true deity of Christ and the authority of Scripture, and his manifest love for the Saviour. Yet Gerhard was a Lutheran of the Lutherans, and on the Lord’s Supper he defended, with all his learning, the bodily presence of Christ’s body and blood under the bread and wine; here we own, gently but without wavering, the Reformed difference, confessing that the sacrament truly conveys Christ to faith by the Spirit, while denying that His body is locally present in or under the elements.
webster_summary: Chief Lutheran scholastic (1582–1637 AD); professor at Jena; author of the nine-volume Loci Theologici.
webster_full: JOHANN GERHARD, proper noun. German Johann (“John”) + Gerhard (“brave with the spear”).
German Lutheran scholastic theologian (1582–1637 AD); professor at the University of Jena.
Third in the classical Lutheran triad after Luther and Chemnitz; counselled in youth by Johann Arndt.
Author of the monumental nine-volume Loci Theologici and the devotional Sacred Meditations.
Defended the Lutheran bodily presence in the Supper — here the Reformed part company.

Psa 63:1

corruption_summary: A learned and devout Lutheran divine, honored for his labour; the Reformed differ from him only on the bodily presence in the Supper.
corruption_paragraphs: Gerhard held no postmodern error, and what must be named in our voice is the honest confessional line that runs between the Lutheran and the Reformed on the Lord’s Supper. With all the weight of his enormous learning he defended the Lutheran doctrine that the very body and blood of Christ are received orally, in, with, and under the bread and wine. We honor his zeal for the reality and comfort of the sacrament, yet we confess with the Reformed churches that Christ’s glorified body is in heaven, and that the faithful truly partake of the whole Christ by the working of the Holy Spirit and the instrument of faith, not by any bodily presence in the elements.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle Gerhard recovers for us is the union of head and heart — the wedding of the most rigorous doctrinal labour to the warmest personal devotion, so that his Loci and his Meditations flowed from the same pen and the same faith. An age that pits scholarship against piety, and cold doctrine against living warmth, is rebuked by Gerhard, who proved that a man may be both the sharpest of theologians and the tenderest of worshippers, seeking God early in a dry and thirsty land.

etymology: Latin Martinus — from Mars, the Roman god of war, thus “of Mars, warlike.” The surname Chemnitz is taken from the Saxon town of that name, itself from a Slavic root meaning “stony brook.”
biblical_def: Martin Chemnitz (1522–1586 AD) was the great second-generation Lutheran theologian, so weighty a divine that the proverb ran, “If the second Martin had not come, the first Martin would scarcely have stood” — meaning that without Chemnitz, Luther’s work might not have endured the confusions that followed his death. A man of vast learning who had once thought to give himself to astronomy, Chemnitz was drawn instead into the service of the church, becoming pastor and superintendent at Braunschweig and the chief architect, with Jakob Andreae, of the Formula of Concord (1577), which reconciled the warring Lutheran factions and secured the confessional unity of the Lutheran churches. His most enduring monument is the four-volume Examination of the Council of Trent, a massive, patient, learned dismantling of Rome’s counter-Reformation decrees, in which he answered the canons of Trent point by point from Scripture and the Fathers — a work that served the whole Protestant cause, Reformed as well as Lutheran, against the errors of the papacy. We honor his immense labour, his defence of justification by faith and the sole authority of Scripture, and his services to the truth against Rome. Yet on the Lord’s Supper Chemnitz stood with the Lutherans for the bodily presence of Christ; and here, honoring his labour, we own the Reformed difference plainly, confessing that the believer feeds on Christ by faith through the Spirit, not by any oral eating of His flesh.
webster_summary: The “second Martin” of Lutheranism (1522–1586 AD); author of the Examination of the Council of Trent and co-author of the Formula of Concord.
webster_full: MARTIN CHEMNITZ, proper noun. Latin Martinus (“of Mars, warlike”) + Chemnitz, a Saxon place-name.
German Lutheran theologian (1522–1586 AD); pastor and superintendent at Braunschweig.
Called the “second Martin”; without him, it was said, the first Martin’s work might not have stood.
Chief author of the four-volume Examination of the Council of Trent against Rome’s counter-Reformation.
Co-architect of the Formula of Concord (1577); a Lutheran on the bodily presence in the Supper.

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Joh 6:63
It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.
corruption_summary: A mighty Lutheran defender of the truth against Rome; honored fully, with the Reformed difference owned only on the Supper.
corruption_paragraphs: Chemnitz taught no error of the modern kind; the only matter to be named plainly in our voice is the old confessional line dividing Lutheran from Reformed on the Lord’s Supper. Chemnitz was a firm defender of the Lutheran bodily presence, and we honor the seriousness with which he sought to guard the reality of communion with Christ; yet we confess with the Reformed churches that the flesh profiteth nothing where the Spirit is not, and that the faithful truly receive the whole Christ by faith and the Spirit’s working, not by the mouth of the body.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle Chemnitz recovers for us is earnest contention for the faith once delivered. His Examination of Trent is a monument of patient, thorough, Scripture-saturated controversy, refusing to let a single false decree of Rome pass unanswered, yet never railing where argument would serve. Against a slothful age that will not read, will not answer error, and will not contend, Chemnitz stands as a rebuke and a model — a workman who fought the good fight of faith with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

etymology: Latinized form of the Flemish Antoon de Wale, “of the wall” or “the Walloon”; a Reformed divine of the Low Countries (1573–1639).
biblical_def: Antonius Walaeus was a Reformed theologian of the Low Countries, born at Ghent and driven with his family into exile for the gospel’s sake, who became a pastor at Middelburg and afterward professor of divinity at Leiden. He stood among the orthodox at the great Synod of Dort, where the churches, gathered from many nations, maintained against the Remonstrants the sovereign grace of God in election, in the definite atonement of Christ, in the effectual call, and in the perseverance of the saints. Walaeus is best remembered as one of the four Leiden professors who together composed the Synopsis of a Purer Theology, a clear and ordered summary of the Reformed faith that fed generations of ministers with sound doctrine. He laboured also in the training of men for the mission-fields of the Indies, that the pure preaching of the word might be carried to the nations. When the aged statesman Oldenbarnevelt was led to his death, it was Walaeus who attended him with the comforts of Scripture, so that the same man who contended earnestly for the truth in the assembly was found tender toward a soul at the last. He witnesses that Reformed conviction and pastoral mercy are not two things but one, both flowing from the God who is sovereign and gracious together.
webster_summary: A Reformed theologian of the Low Countries, professor at Leiden, delegate to the Synod of Dort, and co-author of the Synopsis of a Purer Theology.
webster_full: ANTONIUS WALAEUS, a Reformed divine of the Low Countries (1573–1639), born at Ghent and exiled for the faith.
He served as a pastor at Middelburg and then as professor of theology at Leiden.
He sat among the orthodox at the Synod of Dort, which maintained the doctrines of sovereign grace against the Remonstrants.
He was one of the four Leiden professors who composed the Synopsis Purioris Theologiae, a standard summary of Reformed doctrine.
He trained ministers for the churches and for the mission-fields of the Indies, and attended Oldenbarnevelt with the comforts of Scripture at his death.
scriptures: Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
Psa 16:6
The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage.
corruption_summary: A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the union of sound doctrine and pastoral tenderness in one servant of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Antonius Walaeus is a name of the Reformed churches’ ordered labour, and no movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine him. The dictionary records him that the reader may know the Synod of Dort not as a cold dispute but as the church of Christ contending for the very grace by which sinners are saved, and may know its defenders as men who preached, catechized, trained missionaries, and sat by the dying.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that sound doctrine and pastoral mercy are one work, not two. The same Walaeus who held fast the form of sound words at Dort held out the comforts of Scripture to a condemned man at the scaffold. The world imagines that a man firm in the doctrines of grace must be hard, and a man tender toward sufferers must be loose in his convictions; the Reformed pastor is the standing refutation of both, for he loves men because he loves the truth, and the truth he confesses is that God is gracious to sinners in Christ.
roots_summary: From the Flemish de Wale Latinized to Walaeus, the name of a Reformed professor of Leiden and defender of the faith at Dort.

usage: Like Walaeus at Dort, the faithful minister holds fast the form of sound words in faith and love.
The same servant who contends earnestly for the truth may sit tenderly by the bed of the dying.
Reformed conviction and pastoral mercy flow together from the God who is sovereign and gracious at once.

etymology: Latin Johannes — “John,” from Hebrew Yochanan (“the LORD is gracious”). Piscator is the Latin for “fisherman,” a scholarly Latinizing of the German surname Fischer.
biblical_def: Johannes Piscator (1546–1625 AD) was a German Reformed theologian and biblical commentator, long the leading light of the Reformed academy at Herborn in Nassau. A prodigious labourer in the Scriptures, he produced commentaries upon the whole Bible and a fresh German translation, and his exegetical works were widely read and esteemed among the Reformed. In much he was sound and useful, a diligent expositor who served the churches by his patient labour in the text. Yet on one weighty head of doctrine Piscator fell into a real and serious error, which must be named plainly: he denied the imputation of Christ’s active obedience to the believer. Where the Reformed churches confess that Christ, as our Surety, both bore the penalty of the law in His sufferings and death (His passive obedience) and also fulfilled the whole righteous demand of the law in His holy life (His active obedience), and that both together are imputed to us for our justification, Piscator taught that only Christ’s passive obedience — His death and satisfaction — is imputed, while His active obedience was owed on His own account and is not reckoned to us. This is no small matter, for it touches the very ground of the believer’s standing before God; and the Reformed churches, at the Synod of Dort and elsewhere, rightly maintained against him the full and complete imputation of the whole obedience of Christ, active and passive alike, as the sole righteousness in which the sinner is accepted. We honor Piscator’s labour in the Scriptures while marking his error where he erred.
webster_summary: German Reformed theologian of Herborn (1546–1625 AD); a diligent commentator who denied the imputation of Christ’s active obedience — a real error.
webster_full: JOHANNES PISCATOR, proper noun. Latin Johannes (“John”) + Piscator (“fisherman,” for German Fischer).
German Reformed theologian and biblical commentator (1546–1625 AD); professor at Herborn in Nassau.
A prodigious expositor of the whole Bible; produced commentaries and a fresh German translation.
Denied the imputation of Christ’s active obedience — holding only His passive obedience is reckoned to us.
Answered by the Reformed churches, who maintain the full imputation of Christ’s whole obedience.

Php 3:9
And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:
corruption_summary: A diligent Reformed commentator marred by a real error: his denial of the imputation of Christ’s active obedience.
corruption_paragraphs: Piscator’s error must be named, not softened. He held that Christ’s active obedience — His perfect keeping of the law throughout His holy life — was something owed for Himself as a man under the law, and therefore not imputed to believers; only His passive obedience, His suffering and death, he said, is reckoned to us for justification. This cuts at the root of the gospel comfort, for if only the penalty were paid and not the positive righteousness supplied, the sinner would be left merely acquitted of guilt but not clothed in that perfect righteousness which the law requires for life. The Reformed churches rightly answered that Christ, as the second Adam and our federal Head, was not born under obligation to the law for Himself, but voluntarily placed Himself under it for us, and that His whole obedience, active and passive, is one seamless righteousness imputed to all who believe.

This is a genuine doctrinal corruption within the Reformed household, not a matter of tender confessional difference, and it is answered not by appeal to the spirit of the age but by the plain teaching of Scripture: “by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.” The obedience of Christ that justifies is not truncated but entire. We may honor Piscator’s learning and use his commentaries with profit, even as we reject this his error and hold fast, with the Reformed confessions, to the full and glorious imputation of the whole obedience of our Surety — that the believer is found in Him, not having his own righteousness, but the righteousness which is of God by faith.

etymology: Latin Johannes — “John,” from Hebrew Yochanan (“the LORD is gracious”). Maccovius is the Latinized form of his Polish name, Jan Makowski, taken from his Polish homeland.
biblical_def: Johannes Maccovius (1588–1644 AD) was a Polish-born Reformed scholastic theologian and long-serving professor at the University of Franeker in Frisia, one of the most rigorous and technically precise minds of early Reformed orthodoxy. Trained in the sharp logical method of the schools, Maccovius laboured to give the Reformed faith a rigorous, ordered, and defensible form, wielding the tools of Aristotelian logic and scholastic distinction in the service of sound doctrine. He was a strong and uncompromising defender of the doctrines of grace — the sovereignty of God in election, particular redemption, and the perseverance of the saints — and his precise handling of these truths, though it drew upon him charges of excessive subtlety and even the suspicion of harshness from gentler brethren, was vindicated at the Synod of Dort, where his orthodoxy was examined and upheld. His works on theological method and disputation, and his defence of the high Calvinist doctrine of the divine decrees, made him a formative figure in the tradition of Reformed scholasticism that flowered at Franeker and Leiden. We honor his zeal for the truth, his defence of sovereign grace, and his labour to think clearly and speak precisely about the deep things of God, remembering that the sharpness of the schools, rightly used, is a servant of the gospel and not its enemy, so long as the head that reasons is joined to a heart that worships.
webster_summary: Polish-born Reformed scholastic (1588–1644 AD); rigorous professor at Franeker, defender of sovereign grace.

corruption_summary: A faithful Reformed scholastic, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the right use of rigorous thought in the service of sovereign grace.
corruption_paragraphs: Maccovius held no error worth naming as corruption; his orthodoxy was tried at Dort and vindicated. What is sometimes charged against him is not false doctrine but a certain sharpness and severity of manner, an appetite for logical precision that his gentler brethren feared might chill the warmth of piety. This is a caution about temper and tone, not an accusation of heresy, and it belongs to the man’s character rather than to any corruption of the faith.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle Maccovius recovers for us is the lawful and holy use of the mind in the service of God. A soft and sentimental age despises precise theology as cold, and prefers feeling to formulation; but Maccovius reminds us that we are commanded to hold fast the form of sound words, and that clear, ordered, careful thinking about the deep counsel of God is a servant of worship, not its rival. His example teaches that the sharpness of the schools must be joined to a humble heart bowed before the God whose thoughts are higher than ours — rigorous in the head, reverent in the heart.

etymology: French André — from Greek Andreas (“manly, brave”), the name of the apostle Andrew. The surname Rivet is of French origin, borne by his Huguenot family in the Poitou region of western France.
biblical_def: André Rivet (1572–1651 AD) was a French Huguenot Reformed theologian, pastor, and professor, who after long service to the Reformed churches of France became a professor at the University of Leiden and afterward tutor and governor to the household of the House of Orange in the Netherlands. A man of solid learning and mature piety, Rivet laboured as a controversialist in defence of the Reformed faith against the errors of Rome, writing against the Roman doctrines of the canon, of tradition, and of the sacraments, and upholding the sole and sufficient authority of Holy Scripture. He was esteemed for his sober judgment, his pastoral wisdom, and his irenic yet firm spirit, seeking the peace and unity of the Reformed churches without compromise of the truth. His commentaries and controversial writings served the churches of the Low Countries and beyond, and his counsel was widely sought. In his last illness he left a moving record of a faithful man’s dying, meditating upon the mercy of God in Christ and the sure hope of the resurrection. We honor his steadfast Reformed doctrine, his defence of the authority of Scripture against Rome, his pastoral care, and above all the manner of his death, in which the doctrines he had defended in life became the very consolation of his soul, teaching us that sound divinity is not a cold thing but a living comfort in the valley of the shadow.
webster_summary: French Huguenot Reformed theologian (1572–1651 AD); professor at Leiden and defender of Scripture against Rome.

corruption_summary: A faithful Reformed witness, not a contested doctrine; his life and death recover the truth that sound doctrine is a living comfort.
corruption_paragraphs: Rivet taught no error to be named as corruption; he was sound in the Reformed faith, sober in judgment, and irenic without compromise. The chief threat to his memory is only that so faithful and useful a labourer, who served the churches by his controversial writings against Rome and his pastoral care, should slip quietly into oblivion for want of the fame that attaches to more contentious or colorful men.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle Rivet recovers for us is that sound doctrine is meant to be lived and to comfort us in dying. His careful defences of the authority of Scripture against Rome were no dry academic exercise, for in his last illness those very truths became the consolation of his soul as he meditated on the mercy of God in Christ and the sure hope of the resurrection. Against every notion that doctrine is cold and cannot warm the heart, Rivet’s deathbed answers, teaching us that precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of His saints, and that the faith we defend in health is the faith that carries us through the valley of the shadow.

etymology: Dutch Klaas — a shortened form of Nicolaas (Nicholas), from Greek Nikolaos (“victory of the people”). The surname Schilder is Dutch for “painter” or, in older usage, “shield-maker.”
biblical_def: Klaas Schilder (1890–1952 AD) was a Dutch Reformed theologian, pastor, and professor at the Theological School of Kampen, a vigorous and independent mind in the tradition of the Dutch Reformed churches. A man of powerful intellect and forceful pen, Schilder wrote widely on theology, culture, and the Christian’s calling in the world, most memorably in his profound trilogy meditating upon the sufferings of Christ, tracing the Saviour through His trial, His cross, and His death with rare depth and reverence. When the Nazi occupation fell upon the Netherlands, Schilder used his pen boldly against the tyranny and the false ideology of National Socialism, and for this witness he was imprisoned by the German occupiers and afterward forced into hiding for the remainder of the war — a suffering borne for conscience and for Christ. Amid these trials came also a painful ecclesiastical rupture: over disputes touching baptism, covenant, and church order, Schilder was deposed by the synod of the Reformed Churches in the Netherlands, and he became the leading figure of the churches that separated in what is called the Liberation of 1944, contending for the freedom of the churches from what he judged to be synodical overreach and doctrinal binding beyond the confession. We honor his courage against the Nazi occupier, his rich meditation on the Passion of our Lord, and his zeal for the liberty and purity of Christ’s church, while leaving the particular disputes of the Liberation to be weighed, as all such things must be, by the standard of Scripture and the Reformed confessions.
webster_summary: Dutch Reformed theologian (1890–1952 AD); Kampen professor, leader of the Liberated churches, imprisoned under the Nazi occupation.

corruption_summary: A faithful and courageous witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the calling to obey God rather than men and to meditate upon Christ’s sufferings.
corruption_paragraphs: The chief matter to be marked in Schilder’s life is not a modern corruption but a painful ecclesiastical rupture, the Liberation of 1944, in which he was deposed over disputes touching baptism, covenant, and church order, and led out the churches that separated. We do not here adjudicate every particular of that division, which touched fine questions of covenant and synodical authority; such things must be weighed by Scripture and the Reformed confessions rather than by the passions of party. What is clear and honorable is his contention for the liberty of the local church against binding beyond the confession, and this zeal for the church’s freedom under Christ we may honor even where brethren still differ over the particulars.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle Schilder recovers for us is the courage to obey God rather than men, whatever the cost. When the Nazi occupier came with its false and idolatrous ideology, Schilder did not trim his witness for safety but wrote against the tyranny and bore imprisonment and hiding for it. His trilogy on the sufferings of Christ shows the wellspring of that courage: a soul that had gazed long upon the Man of sorrows, despised and rejected, learned to follow in His steps and count persecution the ordinary portion of all that will live godly in Christ Jesus.
